scenes.tts: Why don't siblings look exactly alike, even with the same two parents? Every child gets half of their chromosomes from each parent. Yet brothers and sisters almost never get the same mix. The answer is in how eggs and sperm are made.
scenes.visual: Two parents above three children, each child made of half mother and half father; question marks over the children; the question, then egg and sperm labels under the parents.
scenes.narration: Why don't siblings look exactly alike, even with the same two parents? Every child gets half of their chromosomes from each parent. Yet brothers and sisters almost never get the same mix. The answer is in how eggs and sperm are made.

scenes.tts: A typical cell in your body has 46 chromosomes, in 23 pairs. You got one chromosome of each pair from your mother and one from your father. A cell with two sets of chromosomes is diploid. A cell with one set is haploid. In humans, a gamete, an egg or a sperm, is haploid, with 23 chromosomes.
scenes.visual: A model cell with three chromosome pairs, blue from mother and orange from father; a small gamete cell with one chromosome of each pair appears beside it.
scenes.narration: A typical cell in your body has 46 chromosomes, in 23 pairs. You got one chromosome of each pair from your mother and one from your father. A cell with two sets of chromosomes is diploid. A cell with one set is haploid. In humans, a gamete, an egg or a sperm, is haploid, with 23 chromosomes.

scenes.tts: Meiosis is cell division that makes haploid cells from a diploid cell. First, the cell copies its D N A once. Each chromosome is now two identical copies, called sister chromatids. Then the cell divides twice. In the first division, the two chromosomes of each pair are pulled apart. In the second, the sister chromatids separate. Usually, four cells form.
scenes.visual: The model cell copies each chromosome, divides into two cells as the pairs separate, then into four cells as the copies separate.

scenes.tts: Meiosis mixes alleles in two ways. An allele is one version of a gene. The first way is crossing over. In the first division, the two chromosomes of a pair lie side by side and swap matching pieces. After a swap, one chromosome in your sex cell can carry alleles from both your mother and your father.
scenes.visual: Two large chromosomes with allele bands lie side by side and swap their lower pieces; one chromosome now carries both colours.
scenes.narration: Meiosis mixes alleles in two ways. An allele is one version of a gene. The first way is crossing over. In the first division, the two chromosomes of a pair lie side by side and swap matching pieces. After a swap, one chromosome in your sex cell can carry alleles from both your mother and your father.

scenes.tts: The second way is independent assortment. Each pair lines up and separates on its own. A normal sex cell gets one chromosome from each pair. Each pair can send either chromosome, so every pair doubles the number of combinations. Three pairs give two times two times two, which is eight. Humans have 23 pairs, so one parent can make two to the power twenty-three combinations, about eight point four million.
scenes.visual: Three pairs; a sex cell takes one from each; the combinations double with each pair to eight; then 2 to the 23 and about 8.4 million.

Each pair can send either chromosome, so every pair doubles the number of combinations. Three pairs give 2 × 2 × 2, which is 8. Humans have 23 pairs, so one parent can make 2²³ combinations, about 8.4 million.

scenes.tts: Fertilization is when an egg and a sperm join. Their two sets of 23 make a diploid cell with 46 again. Each sibling grows from a different egg and a different sperm. Each of those sex cells is a new mix. Meiosis halves the chromosomes and shuffles them, so siblings differ.
scenes.visual: Egg and sperm join into a diploid cell; three children each built from a different egg and sperm look different; the answer in two words.
